paragraphs.heading: Above the mesosphere
paragraphs.text: The thermosphere is the layer of Earth's atmosphere just above the mesosphere and below the exosphere. Its name comes from the Greek word for heat, and it begins about 80 km above sea level. Its upper border, the thermopause, separates it from the exosphere, which begins about 600 km up and is where the atmosphere turns into outer space. By the definition of the Kármán line, set at 100 km, most of the thermosphere already counts as space.

paragraphs.heading: Hot gas that feels cold
paragraphs.text: Temperatures here rise with height, because the gas absorbs highly energetic radiation from the Sun. They depend strongly on solar activity and can climb to 2,000 °C or more, and the very thin gas can reach 2,500 °C. Yet an object in the thermosphere would feel cold. The gas is so sparse, practically a hard vacuum, that its molecules cannot conduct heat to it. At night a normal thermometer would read well below 0 °C, since it would lose more energy by radiating than it picks up by touching the gas.

paragraphs.heading: Charged air and radio
paragraphs.text: Ultraviolet light breaks molecules apart and ionizes them, creating ions, so the bulk of the ionosphere lies inside the thermosphere. Because radiation leaves the particles here electrically charged, radio waves can be refracted by them and picked up beyond the horizon. The Sun's X-rays and extreme ultraviolet light, at wavelengths below 170 nm, are almost entirely absorbed in this layer.

paragraphs.heading: Gases sorted by weight
paragraphs.text: Below the turbopause, at about 90 km, turbulence keeps the air a well-mixed blend whose composition does not change, dominated by nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂). Above it, the gases separate according to their molecular mass, each thinning with height at its own rate. Above about 200 km, lighter gases take over one after another: atomic oxygen (O), then helium (He), then hydrogen (H). Their balance shifts with location, time and solar activity.

paragraphs.heading: Very little mass
paragraphs.text: The density of the atmosphere falls off almost exponentially as you go up. About 80 percent of the atmosphere's mass sits in the troposphere, while everything above about 85 km holds only 0.002 percent of it. With so little mass, the thermosphere cannot be expected to send any significant energy back down to the layers below.

paragraphs.heading: Silence and space stations
paragraphs.text: Above 160 km, in what is called the anacoustic zone, molecules meet so rarely that sound cannot travel. The way this layer moves is dominated by atmospheric tides, driven mainly by daily heating. The thermosphere has no inhabitants except two space stations. The International Space Station orbits in the middle of it, 408 to 410 km up, and the Tiangong station orbits between 340 and 450 km.
